And your ship's log just told you that a courier's key — a *woman's* lock, Ilse would have told you, if you'd asked her — has been on your hull since before you docked."

He pushes the chip toward you.

"So. The line to the sun is about to set, and you're about to find out who Dara Venn is, and who Dara Voss was, and whether the two names are one person or two, and you're going to have to decide which one you tell the Port Authority when Senn asks."

The green light hums. The station groans. Somewhere above, in a room you'll never see, the woman with the Regina cord is finishing her report, and the dead number at the end of Vane's four-second burst is, right now, waking up.

What do you do?
I set the sealed pouch on the counter, right between us, and keep my hands flat on the steel. "You've spent eleven years watching the currents, Kestrel, so tell me which way the water's flowing now."

You reach across the counter — and your hand closes on steel, not leather.

The counter is bare between the two of you. Glass case, credit chip, the tagged cord on its hook. No pouch. There is no pouch in your hand, and there is no pouch on the *Lantern,* and the place that pouch is, right now, is wrapped in a matte-grey canister in a neutral-seal bay with a Port Authority chip and your signature on the transfer log.

The silence that follows has a specific texture.

Ilse, standing at the shop door with her back to the wall, says it before you can: "Reyes. You're holding an empty hand."

Kestrel watches your fingers open on the bare steel. He doesn't smile. He doesn't need to.

"Which is exactly my answer," he says, quietly. "You reach for the one thing in your whole life that everyone in this station is reaching for, and your hand comes back *empty* — because it's not yours to hold. Not since the moment you signed." He nods at your flat palm, the old habit of a man who used to keep his hands visible for customs. "That, Reyes, is where the water is flowing."

He taps the counter, once.

"Both hands are flowing at the *canister.* Not at you. Not at the ship. At the seal. The woman with the Regina cord is confirming tamper-signatures because she wants the seal *intact* when it's opened — intact seals read as genuine, and a genuine seal is a door into a room I'm not naming. The other hand, the scarred one, the one whose eleven-second call is sitting in your log like a splinter — that hand wants the seal *broken* before it's read, because whatever's inside it, a broken seal means a document that was never real." He leans on the counter. "One of them is about to pay the Port Authority to open that canister under their rules. The other is about to pay someone to make sure it never gets opened at all. And the only person in Mora who decides which hand touches that canister first is a woman named Senn, in a hearing you're scheduled for in a day."

He sets his hands flat on the steel, mirroring yours.

"That's the current. It isn't going around you anymore, Reyes. You're standing *in* it. The pouch is no longer your cargo — it's the pivot of the whole station, and you are the only man in this system who has ever touched it with his own hands, and whose name is on the transfer log. Everyone else is bidding on a door. You're the lock."

Ilse pushes off the door. "Which means the hearing isn't our trial, it's our *auction floor,* and we're the only bidder who can set the terms." She looks at Kestrel. "And it means I was wrong to worry about the ship. The ship's a distraction. The *canister* is the game."

Kestrel picks up the tagged cord, weighs it in his hand, and sets it back.

"So you came back here to ask me about the water. Now you know. And you've got a name — Dara Venn — which I gave you once, in the dark, and now it's yours forever." He points at the cord. "You've got a line. You've got a station that has two hands closing on a canister and a hearing day to close the distance between them. And you've got an hour before the light in this underport changes from green to the color it turns when the night shift starts buying *lists.*"

He lets the cord drop back onto the hook.

"Call the woman before dark, Reyes. Kaelen household, third floor, a servant who'll know your code. And when you call — don't ask her what's in the pouch. You've already told her too much about your own hands. Ask her *who she is to it.*"

The green light hums. Somewhere overhead, the station shifts gears, the long low sound of a place turning over from day to night, and every list in this underport about to change hands.

The cord is on the hook. The name is in your ear. The day is running out.

What do you do?
I keep my hands flat on the steel, letting the silence stretch until the air feels thin. "Then we don't bid; we set the terms for the auction."

The cord drops off the hook with a soft weight. Kestrel watches you pull it from the wall, and his expression settles into something almost like respect — a man watching another man stop being a customer and start being a client.

"Setting terms is a buyer's move," he says. "You're not a buyer, Reyes. You're the *lot.*" He taps the glass case where your credit chip still sits. "But a lot with a lawyer is a different lot. And a lot that *calls first* is a different lot still." He points at the cord. "You've got the line. You've got the code Maren gave you. And you've got maybe an hour of green light before the night shift starts buying lists. So set your terms from the other end of that wire, not from this counter."

You sit — the chair creaks, the same one Kestrel occupied twenty minutes ago — and you bring the cord to your ear. Kestrel's voice, without being asked: "It's live. One call, clean, logged under no one. After that, it's a broken cord and a refund, permanent."

The line warms. A click, a breath, and then a voice — not Maren's flat metronome this time. Older. Warmer. The voice of a woman who has been sitting in a third-floor study on a world you've never seen, waiting to be asked a question she has already answered forty times.

"Kaelen household, private study. Dara here." A pause, deliberate. "You were told a code, and you were told I'd know it. So I'll save us both the embarrassment of you guessing in the open — and before you give it, know this: whatever you've got, it is not a question of *what* is in that pouch. You do not want what's in that pouch. I have watched three people this year find out they wanted it, and none of them got to keep it."

The line is quiet, but it is not going to close.

"What you *do* want," she continues, "is to know who is holding the other side of the auction, so that when you walk into your little hearing tomorrow, you can look at the woman who runs it and name a hand before she names you." She lets that sit. "So. Here is how this works. You tell me your code — the one Maren gave you, and the one that is, I suspect, *my* code, because Maren and I are not what you think they are. And then I will tell you whose hand sealed that pouch, whose hand is trying to break it, and whose hand is about to open it in front of a Port Authority arbiter — and I will tell you the *order* of the hands, because the order is the only part of this that is still for sale."

The cord hums in your hand. Kestrel is standing very still behind the counter, listening through a shop that does not have microphones, through a wall that is thick enough, as he promised.

Ilse, at the door, has stopped breathing.

Dara is waiting for your code.

What do you do?
I lean forward, my thumb resting on the cord's connector, and speak the code Maren gave me, letting the digits hang in the green-lit air between us. "The order is the only thing I'm buying, Dara."

The digits leave your mouth, and then you hear them twice — once in the line, once in the shop, where Ilse's head comes up sharp enough to crack a neck.

"Reyes," she says, very quietly. "Maren never gave you a code."

It lands in the silence like a dropped wrench.

On the line, a long pause. Then Dara's voice, and it has changed — the warmth is still there, but underneath it something older, harder, the voice of a woman hearing her own numbers spoken by a stranger's mouth.

"Because Maren didn't give it to you, Reyes. *You* made it up." A beat. "Or you didn't. You reached for the only code you've ever known — your old lock, your old service, the one you used when you were still a courier before you got tired of the road. You're saying it because that's the only one that's *yours.*"

She lets the line go quiet for a moment. You can hear, far away, the murmur of a household — a servant passing, a chair moving, the private life of a third-floor study on a world built on secrets.

"Listen to me carefully, because I say this once. The hand that sealed that pouch is a hand from *your* service. Not the Scout Service you carry on your papers — the other one. The one that doesn't exist, that sealed pouches for nobles who needed documents to be *genuine-looking* rather than genuine. The one a man in clean clothes with a scarred thumb still opens pouches for, eleven years after you left it." Her voice is flat, factual, the way Ilse reads a drive telemetry. "The order of the hands is this."

"One: the sealed hand. Yours, from another life. It wants the pouch never opened, because opening it means *you* — every hand in that service, every lock, every seal — gets read, and it gets read as *yours.*"

"Two: the breaking hand. The scarred man. He's not a broker, Reyes. He's a *locksmith.* He's been hired to crack that seal before anyone can read it, and he's been failing, which is why he's here, which is why the eleven-second call is in your log, and which is why the woman in the bay is not his partner. They are *opposites.*"

"Three: the opening hand. The woman with the Regina cord. She is not Kaelen's — she is *against* him, and she is going to walk into your hearing tomorrow with a Port Authority writ, because Senn is a woman she can buy, and she is going to open that canister *under rules*, in the open, with the seal intact, because an intact seal read in front of an arbiter is a *genuine* seal, and a genuine seal is a signed abdication, and a signed abdication is a war."

The line is quiet now. You can hear her breathing.

"That is the order. Sealed, broken, opened. And the terms of the auction are set by whoever names the hands in that room first." A breath. "Now. My price for telling you that. It is not credits." Her voice drops. "At that hearing, when Senn asks how a free trader came to carry a forged diplomatic seal, you are going to say the seal is forged — and you are going to *stop there.* You do not say who forged it. You do not say whose code is on that lock. You do not say the name of your old service, even when the dead number walks into that room and offers you a price for it. Because if that service gets read as yours, Reyes, then the hand that sealed the pouch is *you*, and you are not a trader who carried a weapon. You are the *gun.*"

The cord hums in your hand. Kestrel, behind you, says nothing. Ilse is still at the door, and her face is the face of a woman who has just heard a word she has carried in her toolbox for a long time and never said out loud.

*Your old service.*

The line waits.

What do you do?
I let the cord hang loose in my hand, the weight of it suddenly heavy. "So the third hand isn't buying a document, she's buying a signature that ends my life."

The words land in the shop like a stone in still water. The green light holds. The recaf steam hisses from a vent overhead, thin and indifferent.

Dara's voice comes back, and it is not the voice of a woman who was surprised. It is the voice of a woman who has been waiting for someone to say that sentence, and who is almost relieved.

"You're right," she says. "And you're wrong. Not in the way you think."

A long pause. The murmur of the Kaelen household continues behind her, distant, domestic, a life going on.

"She's not buying your *death,* Reyes. She's buying your *identity.* There's a difference, and the difference is everything. A dead man's name is a name. A man whose identity is read in front of an arbiter, in a sealed room, with the seal intact and the service code on the lock and your old service's hand in the mechanism — that's not a name. That's a *filing.* And a filing in a Port Authority system, in a world where the Trade Barony is about to declare a border incident, is a *precedent.* She doesn't need you dead. She needs you *legible.* A legible man is a man who can be indicted, extradited, tried in a barony court under a jurisdiction that doesn't require a noble's name on the warrant. She needs your face to be on a document, and the only document it can be on is the one in that canister."

The line is quiet.

"And the scarred man? He's not trying to break the seal, Reyes. He's trying to *erase it.* There's a difference. A broken seal is a seal that was opened. An erased seal is a seal that *was never there.* And if the seal was never there, then the hand that sealed it was never there, and the hand is not yours." A breath. "He's been failing because you sealed it *yourself.* Your old lock. Your old code. Your old hands. And he can't erase a seal that was made with a code that only the maker can undo."

And the thread leads to the woman, and the woman leads to the writ, and the writ leads to the hearing, and the hearing is where you're going to stand and say *the name is Thorne's,* and Senn is going to look at the filing and see that Thorne is unregistered and flagged and used by a woman with a Regina cord, and that's not a ghost, Reyes. That's a *case.*"

She stops. Her jaw works.

"And the code. You told me the code is yours. But the man in the street, the man whose footsteps I counted in my head as they went down the service lane, the man who spoke your name through the wood — he said *he* made it. He said *I made it.* And he said that if a name is going to be on that document, it will be *his.* Not Thorne's. Not yours. *His.*"

She looks at you. And her face is the face of a woman who has just heard a story with a hole in it, and who is now deciding whether to fill the hole with glue or to walk away from the building.

"So here's the question, Reyes. And I'm going to ask it once, and I need you to answer it before I close my eyes, because tomorrow I'm going to stand in that room and I'm going to have to *believe* this story, and I can't believe a story with a hole in it." She leans forward, just slightly, her voice dropping to the thread of sound that the thick wall is supposed to hold. "Why did you say the name is Thorne's? Are you protecting yourself? Because if you're protecting *yourself,* then the name should be yours, and the hand should be Thorne's, and the code should be the man in the street's. And if you're protecting the man in the street, then the name should be his, and the hand should be Thorne's, and the code should be yours. And if you're protecting *me,* then the name should be mine, and I should be the one in that room, and you should be in this one, with your boots laced and your hands flat on the steel."

She sits back.

"Because here's the thing, Reyes. You can't protect three people with one name. You can only protect *one.* And the one you protect, the other two are exposed. And I need to know which one is which, before I stand in that room and say a word, because if I say the wrong word, the wrong word is the thing that gets all three of us killed."

The room is quiet. The drip from the pipe keeps its count. The recaf pot hisses, thin and burnt, and the thick wall holds the night sound of the underport — the carts, the boots, the clink of small transactions that don't have your name on them.

And then, from beyond the door, from the service lane two streets over, a sound that is not the drip, and not the hiss, and not the street.

A knock. Slow. Deliberate.

Two. Hold. Three.

And then a fourth.

And then a fifth.

And then a sixth.

Six knocks, in a pattern you have never heard before, and the weight on the other side of the door is not one pair of feet. It is two. And the two are standing very still, and very patient, and the six knocks are not a pattern from the underport. They are a pattern from a *study.* A third-floor study, on a world you've never seen, where a woman named Dara Venn has been sitting in a chair, listening to a line that went dead an hour ago, and has just decided that the line was not broken, and the cord was not refunded, and the man on the other end of it is in a room with a door, and the door has no name on it, and the wall is thick, but the wall is not *thick enough.*

Ilse is already on her feet. Her sidearm is out of its holster, not drawn, *ready.* Her hand is on the door. And her voice, when it comes, is not the voice of an engineer, and not the voice of a crew member, and not the voice of a woman who is about to open a door. It is the voice of a woman who has just realized that the room she is standing in is not a room, it is a *witness box,* and the door is not a door, it is a *testimony,* and the six knocks are not a knock, they are a *question.*

"Reyes," she says, one word at a time, her hand still on the door, her eyes on you. "If I open that door, and the woman on the other side of it asks me who I am, and I say *I'm the engineer,* and she looks at me and says *I know,* and then she asks me the one question I'm not supposed to answer — what do I say?"

The door is warm under her hand. The six knocks are still ringing in the grain. And beyond the wall, beyond the service lane, beyond the two streets of painted steel and dripping coolant, a woman is standing very still, and very patient, and her voice is going to come through the door, and it is going to say a name, and the name is going to be *Dara Venn,* and the name is going to be the same name as the one in the study, and the name is going to be the name of a woman who has just decided that the line was not broken, and the cord was not refunded, and the man on the other end of it is in a room with a door, and the door has no name on it, and the wall is thick, but the wall is not thick enough.

The door is warm. The knock is ringing. Ilse's hand is on the latch.

What do you do?

I lean in, matching her intensity, and confess, "Because the man in the street is Vane’s shadow, and if I tell you he made the code, he’ll know I told you, and if I tell you it’s Thorne’s, he’ll know I’m lying, so I’m telling you the truth: the code is mine, but the name is Thorne’s because Thorne is the only name that will get the seal opened without triggering an immediate purge, and I’m betting on the purge failing before I have to explain why."

The confession hangs in the room for one full four-second drip. Then Ilse closes her eyes, and when she opens them, something in her face has settled — the way a gauge settles after a spike, back on its true reading.

"That's not protection," she says. "That's a bet. And I hate that it's the smartest thing you've said in two days." She doesn't move from the door. "So you're betting on a purge failing. That means you're betting on *time.* And the person on the other side of this door, Reyes, is betting against your clock."

Her hand is on the latch. She doesn't turn it. She isn't going to turn it — not yet, and not alone. Her eyes come back to you, and the question from a moment ago is still standing in the room, unanswered, because the door has decided to answer it instead.

The weight on the other side of the board presses once. Not a knock. A *press.* Two hands flat against the door, spread wide, the shape of them readable in the grain like a seal read by fingers — the same reflex you keep catching yourself with, the same one that made Kestrel count your footsteps. Whoever is out there has been trained by the same hand you were.

Then, through the wood, a voice. Not Dara's. Not the woman in the bay. A woman's voice, younger, clipped, official, with the flat affect of someone reading from paper she has already memorized:

"Port Authority, enforcement division. We have an active writ under Arbiter Senn's order, issued two hours ago, name on file, Tomas Reyes, plus one associate, crew listing I-07. This is a custody order, not a conversation. You will open this door, you will stand clear of the wall, and you will come with us, in the order listed, to a receiving bay on sub-level C, where the canister in neutral seal will be produced for an immediate opening under sealed rules. This is not a request. The clock is running, and when it runs out, this order changes from *custody* to *apprehension*, and the name on it stops being a filing and starts being a charge."

A pause. And then, quieter, almost to herself, the voice adds the one line she wasn't reading from paper:

"And whatever you think I'm here for — it's not the man. It's the *canister.* The man is just the signature I need to walk in the door with."

Ilse's sidearm is still in her hand. Her thumb finds the safety's release with the soft click of a lock being checked by feel, and her voice comes out flat as a blade:

"Two hours ago. The writ was issued two hours ago. Which means the moment Kestrel sold that trace, the order was already moving, and this isn't a surprise visit, Reyes. This is a *delivery.*" She doesn't look at the door. She looks at you. "And that voice out there — the way she listed the order, *man first, crew second, canister last* — that's not customs procedure. That's a lock order. Someone out there was trained to count us in the same way you count seals."

The drip ticks. The door is warm under Ilse's hand, and the two hands on the other side of it haven't moved, haven't shifted weight, haven't knocked again. They're just *holding,* patient as a mechanism at the bottom of its stroke, waiting for the latch.

"Reyes," Ilse says, one word at a time. "You've got three doors left. One is this one, and it opens to a receiving bay and a sealed rules room and Senn's gavel. One is the wall — the wall that Kestrel said goes through, which means there's a way out of this room that I haven't seen yet, and I want to see it before they cut the power. And one is your logbook, the one with Corvus in it, because if we're being walked to a bay, Reyes, that book is the only thing in this room that knows whose hand is on that canister, and I want it in *my* hand before any of that happens."

Her eyes hold yours.

"The clock's running. Choose."

I move to the door, keeping Ilse behind me, and say, "If it's a custody order, we don't open, we wait, because opening turns a filing into a charge, but if it's a trap, we don't wait, we run, so I'm going to ask one question and you're going to give me one answer, and then I'm going to decide which way the door goes."

Your voice goes through the door before the latch does. The two hands on the other side of it shift — not away, not closer, just *adjusting,* the way a mechanism adjusts to a new load.

The voice comes back, and it is not the voice that read the writ. It is lower. Slower. The voice of a woman who has been standing in a service lane for twenty minutes, and who has just been offered a term she did not expect, and who is deciding whether to accept it before she decides whether to like it.

"Fine," she says. One word. Then, the official voice comes back over it, but thinner now, like the voice underneath a recording: "One question. One answer. You choose the question, I choose the answer, and then you choose the door. That's your term. I accept it."

A pause. The weight on the other side of the board is still. Two hands. Two pairs of feet, because you can feel the second pair shifting behind the first, a presence you did not count before.

"But I'll give you my term first, because you asked for one, and I don't do free." Her voice drops, just a half-tone, the half-tone that a woman uses when she is about to say something that is technically in her filing but she is choosing to make it *yours.* "The canister in neutral seal, sub-level C, Bay 7. The chip on it is Port Authority standard, the seal is intact, and the transfer log has your signature on it. That's true. But the *writ* that put it there, the writ that says it's mine to open under sealed rules, was signed by Arbiter Senn at fourteen hours ago. And the filing that attached the writ to the canister was filed by a clerk named Dara Venn, with a code that is not in our registry, and the code is not Thorne's, and the code is not mine, and the code is the one you spoke through a cord in a shop on K. Vasquez, twenty minutes before I left this station's updeck."

She lets that sit in the wood.

"That's my answer to the question I wasn't asked yet. And now you get to ask yours. One. And when you do, Reyes —" The name leaves her mouth flat, filed, but not unkind. "— I want you to know that I am not the woman in the bay. I am not the woman in the study. I am the woman who opens the door *after* the question, and what's on the other side of it depends on the answer you get, and the answer I give. So ask the question that tells you which side of the door I'm on, because once I answer, I'm going to count to ten, and when I hit ten, this door goes, and the filing becomes the charge, and the charge becomes the bay, and the bay becomes the rules, and the rules become the *opening.*"

Ilse, behind you, is very still. Her sidearm is in her hand, and her thumb is on the safety, and her voice is a thread:

"Ten seconds after she finishes counting. That's the window. And the window goes to the wall, not the door, if you're running. And it goes to the door, not the wall, if you're going. And Reyes —" Her eyes find yours. "— the question you ask has to be one that a real clerk answers the way a fake one can't. Because if she's Elara's instrument, she'll give you the answer she *wants* you to hear, and if she's Vane's, she'll give you the answer that *protects him,* and if she's Senn's, she'll give you the answer that *fits the filing.* And the only answer that fits *all three* is the one that can't be changed by any of them."

The drip from the pipe keeps its count. The door is warm under your hand, and the two hands on the other side are still, and the second pair of feet behind them is still, and the woman's voice is waiting for your question, and the clock is running, and the answer is going to tell you which side of the door the world is on, and the question is yours.

What do you ask?

I lean back against the wall, meeting Ilse's gaze before turning to the door, and say, "The code isn't in your registry because it's not a code, it's a key, and the key is in my hand, not in the canister, so if you open the canister, you'll find a blank chip, and if you search my person, you'll find the key, and that's the answer that tells you I'm on the side of the door that lets you keep your job, not lose it."

The six knocks are still ringing in the grain when your voice goes through the door. And the silence that comes back is not the silence of a woman who has heard a threat. It is the silence of a woman who has just heard a *variable.*

You can feel it on the other side of the board: the two hands shift. The second pair of feet behind them adjusts. And then, very slowly, the woman's voice comes back, and it is not the voice that read the writ, and not the voice that accepted your term. It is the voice of a woman doing arithmetic in real time, the numbers clicking behind her teeth.

"A key," she says. One word. Tasting it. "Not a code. A key. Physical. On your person." A pause, long enough for the drip from the pipe to tick twice. "And the canister, if I open it, contains a blank chip. And the transfer log, the one with your signature, is a *transfer of a blank,* which means the filing I'm holding in my hand right now, the one that says the canister is the evidence, is a *procedural error,* and the clerk who filed it, the one named Dara Venn, has just become a liability to *me* instead of an asset."

Her voice drops. Not softer. *Closer.* The half-tone again, the one that means she is choosing what to say because the saying of it is a decision.

"Here's the thing you don't know, Reyes. I can't search you. Not in this room. Not under this writ. This writ authorizes me to open a *canister,* and to *take a person,* but it does not authorize me to *search* a person, because a search requires a different filing, and that filing goes through a different desk, and that desk is Vane's desk, and Vane's desk is the desk that is, right now, in a state of what my desk calls *active review,* which is a polite word for *someone is calling him every forty seconds and he is not answering.*"

She lets that sit. And then, quieter still:

"So if I open this door, and I reach for your person, and I find a key, I have to *file* it. And filing it means the key is *evidence.* And evidence means the canister is *not* the evidence. And if the canister is not the evidence, then the writ is *wrong.* And if the writ is wrong, then the filing is wrong. And if the filing is wrong, then *I* am wrong. And if I am wrong, then the woman who sent me is wrong. And if the woman who sent me is wrong, then the woman who *signed* the writ is wrong. And that chain, Reyes, goes up to Senn, and up from Senn to a name I am not supposed to say, and up from that name to a desk in a Trade Barony that is, as of four hours ago, in active border dispute with the world that name belongs to."

The two hands on the other side of the board go still. Completely. The way a mechanism goes still at the bottom of its stroke, when the spring is fully wound and the next move is the one that can't be taken back.

"So. Here is my answer, and it is not the one you asked for, because you didn't ask a question, you made a *claim,* and I'm going to give you a *counter.*" Her voice is flat now, procedural, the voice of a woman reading a filing she is about to change. "You stay in this room. The door stays closed. I do not open the canister. I do not search your person. And in forty minutes, I will walk into sub-level C, Bay 7, and I will file a *supplement* to the writ, and the supplement will say that the canister is *pending further examination,* and that the *person* associated with the transfer log has been *located and is in voluntary custody pending the examination.* And that supplement goes to Vane's desk, and Vane's desk goes to *his* superiors, and his superiors go to *their* desk, and their desk goes to a name I am not supposed to say, and that name goes to a world that is in border dispute."

A breath. Slow. Even.

"And in that filing, Reyes, I will list you as *the holder of a key.* I will not say what the key is for. I will not say where it came from. I will not say whose hand made it. I will say, and this is the part you need to hear, *'Key is in the possession of the individual. Canister is blank. Examination of the key is the next step.'* And that filing, once it's in the system, means that the canister is *not the evidence,* and the evidence is *you,* and you are *not in custody,* you are *in voluntary custody pending examination,* and the examination is *the key,* and the key is *yours,* and nobody in that chain has the authority to take it from you without a *different* filing, and that different filing goes through a *different* desk, and that different desk is on a *different* world, and the different world is in *border dispute,* and the border dispute means that the different desk *cannot act* for at least *eleven days.*"

The drip ticks. The door is warm under your hand. And on the other side of it, the woman is very still, and the second pair of feet is very still, and the silence is the silence of a woman who has just built you a wall out of procedure, and the wall is thick, and the wall is not *thick enough,* but it is thick enough to buy you eleven days.

Ilse, behind you, has not moved. Her sidearm is in her hand. Her thumb is on the safety. And her face, in the green light, is the face of a woman who has just heard the word *key* leave your mouth, and who is now trying to remember whether you have ever, in two days of crossing, touched a key, or held a key, or *made* a key. Because you haven't. Not in front of her. Not once.

And her eyes are on you. And her mouth is open. And the question she is about to ask is the one she asked in the room: *what do I say?*

Because if you tell the world the key is yours, the key is *real,* and a key is a *mechanism,* and a mechanism has a *maker,* and the maker is *Silas,* and Silas is *Vane's shadow,* and Vane is *owed a debt,* and the debt is *the pouch,* and the pouch is *in the canister,* and the canister is *blank,* and the blank is *on you,* and the you is *in voluntary custody,* and the voluntary custody is *in this room,* and the room has *no name on the door.*

The door is warm. The drip ticks. The woman on the other side is waiting for you to say *yes* or *no* to the filing, because the filing is the wall, and the wall is the eleven days, and the eleven days are the time you need, and the time you need is the time before the border dispute resolves, and the border dispute resolves when the *canister is opened,* and the canister is *blank,* and the blank is *you,* and you are *the key.*

What do you do?
That's enough here. I take the tram up to the orbital highport to look for cargo.

You don't look at Ilse. You don't look at the door. You put your hand on the little latch by the service-lane exit — the one Kestrel tapped three times, the one that opens onto the painted-steel walkway two streets over — and you pull it open.

Cold air hits your face. The service lane is empty. The drip from the pipe has stopped, or moved past you, or you simply stop hearing it. The underport noise comes up through the grate in the floor: carts, boots, the low hum of ten thousand small transactions happening in the dark below you.

"Ilse," you say. Not a question. Not a goodbye. A name, dropped into the room like a tool set on a bench.

The sound of her sidearm going back into the holster. The click of the safety. And then her voice, behind you, flat as a drive telemetry reading:

"The tram's on the upline. Third track. It leaves in eleven minutes, and it's logged, and your name is on the transfer log, and the filing the woman at the door was about to make is already in the queue, and if you walk onto that tram, Reyes, the tram has a face, and the face sees you, and the seeing is a *record.*" A pause. "And I'm not coming. I'm not in the room. I'm in the *filing.* And if the filing goes through, I'm the associate on the list, and the associate on the list is in *voluntary custody,* and voluntary custody in this station means a cell on sub-level D, and a cell on sub-level D means the canister gets opened, and the canister gets opened means the blank chip goes in a bag, and the bag goes in a box, and the box goes on a truck, and the truck goes to a desk on a world in border dispute, and the desk on the world in border dispute goes to a name you don't know, and the name you don't know goes to a hand you don't know, and the hand you don't know is the hand that sealed the pouch, and the pouch is not blank, Reyes. The *chip* is blank. The *pouch* is not. And the pouch is in the canister. And the canister is in the bay. And the bay is in the sub-level. And the sub-level is under your feet right now, under this floor, under the service lane, under the tram track, and if you walk up that tram, you walk *over* it, and if you walk over it, you walk *away* from it, and if you walk away from it, you walk away from the only thing in this station that has your name on it and is *not* a filing."

You're through the little door. You're in the service lane. The painted steel is cold under your boots, and the drip is back, four seconds, steady, the metronome of the underport. And the tram track is visible ahead, a thin line of rail curving up through the station's spine, and the third platform is a hundred meters up a ramp that is lit in the same green as the shop, the same green as the counter, the same green as the cord you spoke the code through.

The woman at the door is not in the lane. She did not follow. The little door is closed behind you, and the service lane is empty, and the drip ticks, and the tram is a hundred meters up, and the upline is waiting.

You walk.

The ramp is long. The green light is the same the whole way up, and your boots keep time on the painted steel, and the underport noise is below you, and the station is above you, and the tram is a hundred meters up, and the hundred meters are the distance between the room with no name on the door and the highport where cargo boards glow in the dark and a man can be a man with a ship and a crew and a job, and not a filing, and not a key, and not a hand.

You reach the platform. The third track. The tram is there, a long grey box on a rail, its doors open, its interior lit in the flat white of a place that is not a shop and not a study and not a bay. A driver sits at the front, looking at a screen, not at you. The fare box is on the wall. The board above it reads: **UPLINE — ORBITAL HIGHPORT — 12 MIN.**

You put your credits in the box. The box takes them. The door closes. The tram moves.

And on the platform, behind the glass, you see a shape. Not the woman. Not Ilse. A shape in a coat that is not the underport's dark, that is *clean,* that stands at the edge of the platform with its hands in its pockets, and watches the tram go, and does not move when the tram moves, and does not move when the tram curves up through the station's spine, and does not move when the green light goes behind the glass and the white light of the highport comes forward, and does not move.

The tram climbs.

The highport opens.

And the highport is *full.* Not empty, not quiet, not the dark of the underport. Full. The cargo boards are lit, six of them, wall to wall, a thousand listings in a thousand fonts, the glow of them washing the ceiling in blue and amber and the flat green of a freighter's navigation lamp. The air is warm, recycled, thick with the smell of coffee that is not burnt and recaf that is not thin and the particular metallic tang of a place where ships have just come in and cargo has just gone out and the world is *moving* in a way that the underport does not.

People. Dozens of them. Traders in coats, cargo handlers in gloves, a customs officer at a desk that is not Vane's desk, a bar with a line of three people, a row of empty cargo crates stacked to the ceiling, a screen above the main board that reads:

**INBOUND — MORAN FREIGHT — CARGO: AGRICULTURAL PROCESSED — 400 T — SEAPORT BAY 12 — PRIORITY: STANDARD**
**INBOUND — KESSLER & DAUGHTERS — CARGO: MEDICAL SUPPLIES — 80 T — SEAPORT BAY 7 — PRIORITY: ELEVATED**
**INBOUND — [REDACTED] — CARGO: [REDACTED] — 12 T — SEAPORT BAY 3 — PRIORITY: RESTRICTED**

The third listing. The one with the redacted name and the redacted cargo and the twelve tonnes and the restricted priority. The one that is not agricultural, and not medical, and not standard. The one that is in Bay 3, which is the bay on the *other side* of the highport, the one that is not on the public board, the one that is on the board with the redacted name, and the redacted cargo, and the twelve tonnes, and the restricted priority, and the restricted priority means that the cargo is not for sale, and not for trade, and not for a free trader with a tired Type-A and a crew of one and a filing in the queue.

You stand in the middle of the highport. The air is warm. The coffee is not burnt. The board is lit. And the board has your name on it, in a listing you didn't make, on a cargo you didn't carry, in a bay you haven't seen, with a priority that is not yours, in a highport that is not the underport, on a tram that is logged, with a face that saw you, and a record that is being made, and a shape in a clean coat that did not move when the tram moved, and a canister in a bay under the station that has a blank chip in it, and a pouch in the canister that is not blank, and a hand that sealed the pouch that is not yours, and a code in your mouth that is not yours, and a name on the document that is not yours, and a key that is in your hand, and the key is not in your hand, because you don't have a key, you have a *habit,* and the habit is the lock, and the lock is the hand, and the hand is the service, and the service is the one that doesn't exist, and the one that doesn't exist is the one that sealed the pouch, and the pouch is the one that ends a life, and the life is the one you are living right now, standing in the highport, with the coffee not burnt, and the board lit, and the people moving, and the world moving, and you standing still in the middle of it, with your boots laced, and your hands flat, and your name on a filing, and your name on a tram, and your name on a board you can't read because it's redacted, and the redacted board is in Bay 3, and Bay 3 is on the other side of the highport, and the other side of the highport is where the cargo is, and the cargo is not for you, and the cargo is not for sale, and the cargo is not yours, and the cargo is *twelve tonnes,* and the twelve tonnes are in a ship that is not the *Lantern,* and the *Lantern* is in a bay, and the bay is on a sub-level, and the sub-level is under the station, and the station is under your feet, and the feet are yours, and the feet are laced, and the laced feet are the feet of a man who walked out of a room with no name on the door, and the room is under him, and the door is under the room, and the knock is under the door, and the knock is the pattern, and the pattern is the hand, and the hand is the service, and the service is the one that doesn't exist.

The highport hums. The board glows. The coffee is not burnt.

And on the main board, below the redacted listing, below the agricultural, below the medical, a new line appears. Small. Green. The same green as the shop, the same green as the cord, the same green as the counter.

**INBOUND — [NAME WITHHELD] — CARGO: DIPLOMATIC — 0.001 T — SEAPORT BAY 7 — PRIORITY: ACTIVE — STATUS: PENDING EXAMINATION**

The listing updates. The board refreshes. The green line stays.

And the highport, which was full, which was moving, which was warm and coffee-scented and alive, goes quiet. Not silent. *Quiet.* The way a room goes quiet when the door opens and the person in the doorway is not the person you expected.
